main_argument_chains.claim: Ordered prior crime locations can support a bounded next-location priority surface through persistent anchor-point patterning.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Use the surface as a resource-priority input only inside the stated domain and offender scope.

main_argument_chains.claim: Multiple local anchors can reduce wasted high-likelihood area when the sequence has distinct spatial clusters.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Prefer the sharper cluster surface only after specifying weights and reporting catastrophic-miss risk.

main_argument_chains.claim: Retrospective next-event performance can reject an unhelpful spatial method and compare surviving variants.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Treat the mean as an uncalibrated diagnostic, not probability, because the final outlier can dominate operations.

main_argument_chains.claim: Local map knowledge and anchor investigation must complement an abstract likelihood surface.
support_steps: active anchor search versus passive patrol
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Record human changes and choose the prediction target case by case.

warnings.warning: The event-merging rule calls p>0.01 highly statistically significant; the inequality conflicts with the usual small-p convention.
The summary says seven data sets from three criminals, the test-set prose says seven different criminals, and later evaluation says only three complete test data sets.
The flat-baseline multiplier depends on search area and grid definition, so its magnitude is not an invariant measure of practical value.
The three-times search-square rule and more-than-90-percent coverage claim are not estimated or uncertainty-checked on the recovered data.
The Gamma MLE prose asks for r-hat and maximization over theta and r even though the defined parameters are k and theta; the numerical parameter should be k-hat.
The temporal adjustment uses only the last radial difference, with no smoothing, uncertainty, or test that the apparent trend persists.
Figure 6(b) labels an Offender B surface as Offender C.
Singleton silhouettes are described as one and then removed from the average; this differs from common zero/undefined conventions and favors the chosen handling.

Reference 11 visually prints 'In 1005 UK Crime Mapping Conference, 2005,' an apparent bibliographic year/title error.
